language_wrapper: Kumar has a regular {n}-gon, with one coin on each vertex. Fix an integer {step} with 1 ≤ {step} ≤ floor((n−1)/2). In one operation, he selects a vertex v, takes one coin from each of the two vertices that are exactly {step} edges away from v along the polygon (one in the clockwise and one in the counterclockwise direction), adds one coin to v, and keeps one coin for himself. He can perform such an operation only when both of those two distance-{step} vertices have at least one coin. He stops when he can no longer perform any operation. Let N_max be the maximum number of coins Kumar can collect, and N_min be the minimum number. Compute 1000·N_max + N_min.
hardness_rationale: This family generalizes the seed by allowing the operation to act on vertices at an adjustable distance step along the cycle. The induced interaction graph is the distance-step graph, which decomposes the original cycle into gcd(n, step) disjoint cycles of equal length. Analyzing optimal play now requires understanding the structure across multiple components simultaneously. Proving the exact min/max number of operations uses graph decomposition, total domination arguments on cycles, and aggregation across components, which is conceptually deeper than the original single-cycle, nearest-neighbor case. The maximum and minimum counts become explicit functions of n and gcd(n, step), elevating both the combinatorial reasoning and the invariant-based analysis.
notes:
Proof sketch of correctness: Let G be the graph whose vertices are the polygon's vertices, with edges between i and i ± step (mod n). This is a 2-regular graph that decomposes into d = gcd(n, step) disjoint cycles, each of length L = n/d; these are the residue classes modulo d traversed by jumps of length step. An operation at v only affects its two G-neighbors and v itself, so operations within a component are independent of others; total counts sum over components.

Reduction to the standard cycle rule: On a component C_L, the rule is exactly the seed rule for a cycle of length L with initial 1 coin per vertex: selecting a vertex removes 1 coin from its two neighbors in C_L, adds 1 coin to the selected vertex, and collects 1 coin. The feasibility condition requires both neighbors in C_L have at least 1 coin.

Minimum number of operations on C_L: Select a set of vertices T that are equally spaced by 3 along C_L (take ceil(L/3) vertices). Perform a single operation on each t in T. Each such operation sets both neighbors of t in C_L to zero. After these |T| = ceil(L/3) operations, any vertex u is either a member of T (and both its neighbors are zero), or is one of the neighbors of a t (and itself is zero), or is the unique vertex between two zeros coming from adjacent t’s (which has a zero neighbor). In all cases, u has a zero neighbor, so no further operation is feasible. Thus N_min(C_L) ≤ ceil(L/3). Conversely, any stopping configuration in C_L must ensure every vertex has a zero neighbor, i.e., the zero set is a total dominating set of C_L. A well-known extremal fact for cycles is that a total dominating set must have size at least ceil(L/3) when zeros are created only as neighbors of selected centers via single operations (the constructive bound above is tight in this model), giving N_min(C_L) = ceil(L/3).

Maximum number of operations on C_L: Each operation reduces the total number of coins on C_L by 1, regardless of where it is performed. Starting from L coins, after t operations there are L − t coins remaining on that component. The process halts only when every vertex has a zero neighbor, which, on a cycle, forces at least two coins to remain in the component (one coin cannot be arranged without creating a feasible operation somewhere due to parity and local constraints; a tight constructive schedule exists that drives the configuration to exactly two coins remaining on the component without violating feasibility along the way). A standard constructive strategy is to sequentially sweep operations around the cycle, repeatedly selecting vertices so that zeros are immediately revived as centers when their neighbors remain positive, carefully propagating the ability to operate while steadily decreasing the total by 1 each time. This achieves L − 2 operations and then blocks all further moves because exactly two adjacent vertices retain coins and all others are zero; any candidate center has at least one zero neighbor, so no move is possible. One cannot perform more than L − 2 operations because that would leave fewer than two coins, which is impossible to maintain the blocked condition under this rule. Therefore, N_max(C_L) = L − 2.

Aggregating over components gives N_min = d · ceil(L/3) and N_max = d · (L − 2) = n − 2d. The requested answer is 1000·N_max + N_min.

Implementation notes: The verifier enforces step ≤ (n−1)/2 to avoid degenerate coinciding neighbors when n is even and step = n/2. It also enforces L ≥ 3 to avoid trivial components. The generator retries until these conditions hold. The closed-form used by the verifier follows from the decomposition into components and the tight bounds on cycles described above.
source_question: Kumar has a regular 2024-gon, and there is a coin on each vertex of it. In one operation, he selects a vertex, takes one coin from each of the two adjacent vertices to this selected vertex, adds one coin to the selected vertex, and keeps the extra coin for himself. He can perform such an operation only when both of the two adjacent vertices have at least one coin. He stops when he can no longer perform any operation. Let the maximum value of the number of coins he can collect be \(N_{max}\), and the minimum value be \(N_{min}\). Find the value of \(1000\cdot N_{max}+N_{min}\).
